Title: June 11, 2026 City of Boulder City Council Study Session - 2026 State Legislative Session Update

Topic1.Title: Overview of 2026 State Legislative Session and City Advocacy
Topic1.Summary: Heather Staer, intergovernmental affairs officer, reviewed the outcomes of the 2026 state legislative session, which ran January 14 to May 13 and passed around 450 of 626 bills. The city took positions on 58 bills, and the state budget was the defining force of the session. The governor had vetoed 12 bills with a final action deadline the following day.

Topic2.Title: State Budget Shortfall and Impacts on Boulder
Topic2.Summary: The Joint Budget Committee had to cut about a billion dollars, leaving little room for new programs, and Medicaid costs are a major driver of the deficit. Senate Bill 135 refers a question to voters on the Taber cap for K-12 funding, and Senate Bill 187 created a Medicaid commission. The direct hit to the city is the elimination of the local retail marijuana sales tax share, about $150,000, while indirect impacts include cuts to multimodal transportation funds and affordable housing finance funds.

Topic3.Title: Immigration Bills and Federal Response
Topic3.Summary: The majority party focused on responding to federal actions, particularly immigration, and Democrats struggled to unite behind a single path. Of five immigration bills, two were killed in committee and one was vetoed, while House Bill 1276 passed to address civil liability for sharing immigration status information and authorize detention center inspections. Other bills responded to federal challenges to mail-in voting and federal orders keeping coal plants open.

Topic4.Title: Priority Bills: Homelessness, AI and Utility On-Bill Repayment
Topic4.Summary: House Bill 1202 passed, creating multi-jurisdictional homelessness authorities and requiring a state homelessness strategy. Senate Bill 189 on automated decisionmaking passed and clarifies city responsibilities for AI use. Senate Bill 148, the city's utility on-bill repayment program, failed in appropriations despite years of work and will be re-evaluated over the interim.

Topic5.Title: Housing, Land Use and Transit-Oriented Development Bills
Topic5.Summary: Several housing bills the city supported passed, including Senate Bill 40 on affordable homeownership and House Bill 1065 creating transit and housing investment zones with an affordable housing tax credit. House Bill 1224 strengthened protections for mobile home park residents. The city opposed House Bill 1114 on minimum lot sizes and House Bill 1308 on lot splitting, both of which failed in committee.

Topic6.Title: Data Center Bills and Clean Energy Legislation
Topic6.Summary: Dueling data center bills, House Bill 1030 offering incentives without energy requirements and Senate Bill 102 setting strict requirements, both failed, and sponsors are expected to return next session. Clean energy wins included plug-in solar passing and House Bill 1226 on coal units, while Senate Bill 208 removing wind as a clean energy standard was defeated. Staff noted the bills preserved local control.

Topic7.Title: Public Safety Bills and Firearm Safety
Topic7.Summary: The city opposed three major bills that would have eroded local and state firearm safety laws, and all three were defeated. The city supported House Bill 1144 placing guardrails on 3D printing of firearms. These items reflect the city's advocacy in an election year.

Topic8.Title: RTD Board Modernization (House Bill 1150)
Topic8.Summary: The legislature passed House Bill 1150, reducing the RTD board from 15 to nine members with five elected and four governor-appointed, and redrawing districts. The city sought seven elected members, equity language in gubernatorial nominations, and a lower signature threshold, securing only a return to 250 signatures. Requests for more elected seats and equity language were not granted.

Topic9.Title: Looking Ahead: 2026 Election, Leadership Changes and Budget Outlook
Topic9.Summary: The November 2026 election will determine control of the General Assembly, with Democrats likely retaining control but a possible shift between moderate and progressive factions. New legislative leadership and a new governor may change priorities, and the budget may require a special session. Staff expects a budget forecast in mid to late June.

Topic10.Title: November 2026 Ballot Measures Overview
Topic10.Summary: Heather Staer reviewed the ballot measures, including Initiatives 85, 95, 108, 109 and 110 that are officially on the ballot, and the referred measure Senate Bill 135 on retaining revenue above the Taber cap. Initiative 175 on dedicating transportation taxes to roads was expected to be verified soon, and Initiatives 177 and 195 were in circulation. The council may take positions via resolution at a future meeting.

Topic11.Title: Council Discussion of Ballot Measures and Next Steps
Topic11.Summary: Council members raised concerns about Initiatives 95, 108, 109, 110, 85 and 175, noting potential harms to vulnerable communities and state funding, and asked who backs the measures. Council requested staff research and summaries on each measure, including Initiative 175, before deciding whether to take positions by resolution. Staff will bring back additional analysis at a future meeting.

Topic12.Title: Council Questions on Grants, Data Centers and Wildfire-Related Utility Reliability
Topic12.Summary: Council asked about the aggregate fiscal impact of a failed Taber cap increase, the comparative marijuana tax impact on other communities, and data center bill status. Council also asked about collective action on wildfire and power reliability, and staff noted a PUC reauthorization included quality of service plans. Staff said they would look into the grant success rate and monitor state budget forecasts.
